extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and students interested in film censorship and banned films
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and listing the various grounds and justifications given by countries, classification boards, or authorities for banning or censoring films, illustrated with international examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distorting history
rubrics_metrics.description: Films may be banned for 'distorting history' or presenting an historical narrative deemed inaccurate or harmful (example: Child 44 banned in Kazakhstan for distorting history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by states sensitive to portrayals of historical events or national history; grounds often invoked by governments to remove films that conflict with official narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious offence / 'too religious' content
rubrics_metrics.description: Films banned for content judged 'too religious' or otherwise offensive to religious sentiments (example: Egypt reportedly banning The Matrix as 'too religious'; other bans for offending Christianity or Islam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where authorities view material as violating dominant religious norms or as proselytising/offending a faith; can lead to outright bans or demands for cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually explicit content / adult pornography
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexually explicit scenes or pornographic material can be grounds for banning or removal (examples: sexually explicit films pulled in Egypt; Fifty Shades blocked in some countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification boards and moral authorities frequently restrict exhibition of explicit sexual content; may be framed as protecting public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBTQ+ content (same‑sex kissing, homosexuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of same‑sex affection, LGBTQ+ relationships or themes has led to bans in multiple countries (examples: Lightyear banned over a lesbian kiss; Barbie/other films banned/blocked for 'homosexuality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common reason for bans in conservative jurisdictions; sometimes results in refusal to screen, demands for cuts, or national-level prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of transgender actors or transgender themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of transgender actors or explicit transgender content has been cited as a reason to block screenings (example: Talk to Me banned in Kuwait over inclusion of a trans actor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to LGBTQ+ grounds but sometimes cited specifically; can trigger bans even when content is not sexually explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence to national/political sensibilities / insulting a people or nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Films judged to insult a nation, people, or national sensibilities (e.g., 'insulting Iraqis') or portray a country negatively have been removed or banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often invoked after public backlash or by governments seeking to prevent perceived national insult; may target depictions of events, leaders, or social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor nationality / political boycott reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Films have been banned because of an actor's nationality or political associations (examples: Wonder Woman, Death on the Nile and other films blocked in Lebanon/Kuwait due to Gal Gadot's Israeli nationality or IDF past).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how extratextual factors (cast/crew nationality or politics) can become grounds for censorship under boycott or political protest rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political content: anti‑government, anti‑clerical or sensitive political themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Films critical of governments, clerical establishments, or dealing with sensitive political events (assassinations, massacres, war documentaries) are frequently censored or banned (examples: anti‑cleric films, documentaries on East Timor/Aceh, Jenin Jenin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may argue such films threaten public order, national security, or stability; bans may be legal (court orders) or administrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive/Gratuitous gore and violent content
rubrics_metrics.description: Films deemed to contain gratuitous gore, extreme violence, or shocking imagery (examples cited: Cannibal Holocaust, Human Centipede 2, I Spit On Your Grave, references to 'gratituitous gore') are often refused classification or banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification offices assess violence levels; excessive depictions can lead to refusal of classification, legal prohibition, or mandatory cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child sexual content / child pornography
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sexual depiction involving minors or material meeting legal definitions of child pornography triggers criminal concerns and bans (text references to child pornography law/procedure and Dutch Penal Code section 240b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are often absolute legal prohibitions; classification bodies and criminal law restrict distribution/exhibition with severe penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectionable / morally offensive content (broad category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification as 'objectionable' (a legal/administrative label in some jurisdictions) for moral, indecent or offensive content can justify bans (e.g., OFLC decisions listing works as objectionable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Umbrella term used by classification boards to capture a range of grounds (sex, violence, hate speech); leads to prohibition of distribution/screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious or cultural morality (public decency / unacceptable behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Films restricted for violating local standards of decency, morality, or 'acceptable behaviour' (examples: bans citing 'unacceptable behavior' or offense to religion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoked to protect community standards; scope varies widely by country and may overlap with religious offence and sexual explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat to regime legitimacy / national security concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities may ban films perceived to threaten regime legitimacy or national security (examples: North Korea restricting certain films fearful of undermining state narratives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often cited in authoritarian states where cinema is controlled as part of political stability; justification can be vague and broadly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship for local cultural/political context (examples by country)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many bans are specific to local cultural, legal, or political contexts—e.g., bans tied to local events, religious majorities, or regional laws (numerous country‑by‑country examples are listed: Egypt, Kuwait, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Iran, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that reasons and thresholds for banning vary by jurisdiction; what is permissible in one country may be prohibited in another.
